finding: Three of the mechanisms are genuinely in use - session setup with a capability set read back as negotiated, in-turn frames consumed as they arrive (11 update frames, none after the terminal frame), and a closed typed stop-reason set the conformance run branches on per adapter. Two are not: no permission request is raised or answered anywhere in the repository (0 call sites) even though every session in every example negotiates permission_callbacks true, and session restoration is explicitly not served for the turn. The update stream also stops at the boundary - TurnResult carries a frame count and not the frames, so both consuming examples rebuild step.progress events from that count after the turn has finished, which is the questionnaire's own description of updates synthesised after the fact - and the only adapter that speaks real protocol method names has never been executed and folds max_tokens and refusal into end_turn.
gap: An answer_permission_request operation on the built interface (the capability's own contract already lists it), with a request actually raised by at least one adapter and answered from policy in a non-interactive run; frames delivered to the caller rather than counted, carrying tool-call status as well as text; and a stop-reason set that does not collapse max_tokens and refusal into end_turn. A written list of which protocol methods are implemented, stubbed or refused, with the reason for each, does not exist outside two lines of the harness provenance.

evidence.quote: the agent control protocol itself revises to a new major version, as distinct from swapping which runtime speaks it
every agent-runtime adapter at once, because the turn and stop-reason shapes are the protocol's, not the runtime's
No product name appears in this file.
Define the interface over the turn only and keep the binding out of the contract, so a remote binding arrives as an adapter rather than as a change to the shapes.

finding: The build owns the turn shapes, a closed four-value stop-reason set and an RFC 9457 failure registry; the protocol is a transport one adapter speaks, mapping its own stopReason onto that set, over stdio or a unix socket, with no product name above the adapters and a product scan that fails the gate if one appears. The exit is written rather than implied: a named impact row says a new major version of the protocol moves every runtime adapter and the conformance run while the core is unaffected, and names the harness test, and the capability's open question defaults to keeping the binding out of the contract so a remote transport arrives as an adapter. Not leading: the written exit is not exercised - no second protocol or remote binding has ever been served here, the second adapter speaks no protocol at all, and the impact row's own wording still calls the turn and stop-reason shapes the protocol's while the interface in fact defines its own narrower set.
